The ending was sweet. I think it was an interesting story they were trying to tell. & you know A24 is gonna do it in a non straight forward way. I didn’t think it was bad, a little trippy though with the mix of shots of reality mixed thoughts sometimes crazy ones. On Charlie’s side I think they were trying to show some type of obsession & what that does after a prolonged time with no proper outlet. With Emma, I think they were trying to show the limits of human thoughts before executing on it. In a more straightforward way the movie literally talks about how many people we know or interact in society that have planned something heinous but didn’t go through with it. Like a school shooting. I think it’s interesting because most people would keep those dark thoughts to themselves no matter what. You know like the saying “even batman wouldn’t get this info outta me”. So the fact the Emma shares this evil intention of a school shooting with the group, and you see how the characters divulge after it is truly interesting. Especially because in real life I think people would be too guarded to even share information as sensitive as that.

This movie was so disappointing to me because it was so stylized and tonally interesting that I kept anticipating something ~greater~ and more provocative from the plot. I understand that gun violence is not the point nor the discussion presented in the movie, but wow what a shallow and half-baked thematic exploration about morality and the capacity for change without tapping into any of its potential conversations it could have had about women, the psyche, and mass scale violence like this. I saw someone call this an “almost European take on gun violence discourse” (again, knowing that the point of this movie has nothing to do with gun violence) and I couldn’t agree more. Just a really flat, shallow arc. Zendaya’s character is portrayed as very sweet, demure, and shy, and so once the rising plot action was presented I expected something innovative and profound. Once I knew where the plot was going, I was SO BORED and genuinely said “oh that’s it. Someone read this script and decided to fund it.” Out loud. It gets two stars because I loveeee the visual storytelling and how this is shot. I think Zendaya and RP have such good on screen chemistry and want to see them together again. Idk babes… this could have gone anywhere and went nowhere. It was just so FLAT.

Maybe (definitely) I am too demanding when it comes to cinema and maybe (for sure) I am too strict with my ratings, but the plot was just not it. I was not too shocked by the plotwist because I already knew the film's premise so that surely changed my perspective of it, as well as the surprise-effect. Despite of these complaints, I love every single movie that makes me reflect about what I just watched, even if it might be a stupid and useless consideration. The way the story develops is absolutely absurd in my opinion, but still I caught it as an irrational metaphor for all the trust and stability issues that concern marriage. I am a bit disappointed by the fact that they probably added Charlie's cheating as a quicker and easier resolution in order to put him in a bad light and to help the audience being more empathetic with Emma. It worked indeed, even though the actions can't be compared, at least solely based on their objective nature. By highlighting the couple's mistakes (and exaggerating them till their limits) the story shows that no one is perfect, wether it be the most scenical or daily actions. Regarding Rachel's character, I've read so much hate towards her. Of course we cannot forget that she ruined someone's wedding, but anyway it seemed like Charlie and Emma's relationship was already on thin ice, so I wouldn't address all the responsibility on her. She might be an incoherent woman and a vendicative friend. At least she was right about one thing though: they're perfect for each other... because they're both equally mad, I would add. The ending saved the film. Totally expected and plain. However, exactly what I wanted to see.

“What’s the worst thing you’ve ever done?” That question is the catalyst for the titular drama in Kristoffer Borgli’s fourth feature film. I’ve only seen Sick of Myself before this, and Borgli certainly has a unique style and a certain type of feel connecting these films. That is overthinkers and the anxiety of how we are seen in the modern world. Borgli uses rapid editing, extreme close-ups, an unrelenting score, and my personal favorite in both these films, the worst-case scenarios our protagonists envision in their minds. This time around, though, I think Borgli is coming from a much warmer place, yet this film still has the unnervingly awkward humor that he’s really mastered. This film is about how the almost picture-book romance between Emma and Charlie we see in the opening sequence of the film is completely recontextualized once Emma reveals the worst thing she’s ever done. However, I would say what the film is really doing is showing what the worst thing Charlie has done is and his whole process leading up to it, which he was unable to answer when first asked. He completely fails to give Emma the proper empathy in this situation and lets his biggest questions fester in his head until it completely breaks him, leading him to fantasize about Emma’s past and make up false narratives about why instead of listening to her and seeing the person she has grown into. He even goes as far as deleting his entire speech about all the things he loves about her and cheating on her. Yet we do empathize with him while he is making every horrible decision possible in this film because, yes, learning what we do about Emma does fundamentally change how he sees her and how we, the audience, do. Emma is not given the grace that the other players of their game are. While both Rachel and Mike’s stories resulted in real harm, the societal taboo of Emma’s plan makes everyone immediately turn on her. I think the first question they should have asked Emma is why she didn’t go through with it. Instead, she is ostracized by Rachel, who shows her lack of growth from her adolescence, and Alana Haim does a great job portraying this mean-girl, holier-than-thou energy that I’m sure Emma had to deal with before. Also, you gotta feel bad for Mike cause he genuinely seems like a chill dude. Back to Emma, though, because as she and Charlie discuss it, we can understand the why, even if there never really is a why in these scenarios. Emma was young, lonely, insecure, new in a town with no friends, and bullied, and as she says, the aesthetic is what captured her, which I think is a common case for a lot of people in her shoes. Now, when the actual shooting happens in her town, Emma is confronted with the reality of the situation, and we see she’s not a psychopath but just alone, and she uses the tragedy to make friends. She starts protesting, and like she says to Charlie, it wasn’t her being a poser but waking up from her bad dream and escaping her fantasy, which does lead her to be the person Charlie writes about in the beginning. I think Charlie also comes to that conclusion in the end as he tries to deliver his speech at the wedding but completely collapses under all the stress he caused himself, which results in an incredibly cringeworthy but hilarious scene as he tries to communicate all those things about Emma, but instead he pukes out all his thoughts, ruining their wedding night and getting his ass kicked. In the end, though, we get this beautiful scene of Charlie going to the diner where Emma asked to go on their wedding night alone when he initially blew off the idea. This is where we see the difference between Emma and Charlie and why they are perfect for each other, as Emma also walks into the diner, orders her cheeseburger, and sits down with Charlie. And she does what Charlie couldn’t: start over and give Charlie a second chance, which is what I think the film is really trying to say. When you truly love someone, it means giving them a chance to improve with support to be better, which is what Charlie doesn’t do for their wedding DJ, which sets off this whole mess, and then they are stuck with this horrible DJ in the end. Also, the acting from Zendaya and Pattinson is phenomenal. I love what they are doing with their faces in this, reacting to everything. They also both give us such insight and empathy for these characters. Also, their chemistry is great in this, especially that opening sequence. Also, shoutout to Hailey Benton Gates for being a baddie in this. But yeah, The Drama is a hilariously cringeworthy but empathetic look into love and the baggage we all carry and hide from others.

The drama mi ha spiazzato perché mi aspettavo una cosa e invece me ne sono trovata un'altra molto più gradita. Cosa c'è di più pesante di scoprire qualcosa della persona che stai per sposare che ti lascia spiazzato e ti fa completamente cambiare prospettiva verso di lei? Nulla credo, e questo film ti fa sentire lungo tutta la durata proprio i sentimenti di confusione che provano dentro i due protagonisti (interpretati da due perfetti Robert Pattinson e Zendaya). L'intuizione brillante del regista non sta tanto nel segreto in sé — la confessione di Emma di aver pianificato una strage scolastica in gioventù, atto poi mai compiuto ed espiato attraverso un successivo attivismo contro le armi — quanto negli effetti psicologici che questa rivelazione scatena. Il passato non serve a giustificare il presente, ma diventa il detonatore di una crisi d'identità relazionale. Charlie si ritrova improvvisamente a convivere con una sconosciuta, ed è qui che il film scava un solco profondo nello spettatore: chi è davvero la persona che abbiamo accanto?In questo scenario, il film rifiuta saggiamente di dividere il mondo in buoni e cattivi. Non c'è un colpevole univoco. questa storia è una radiografia dell'ipocrisia umana: mostra con quanta spaventosa rapidità siamo disposti a revocare l'amore e la stima verso qualcuno, dimenticando anni di vita condivisa a causa di un singolo frammento del passato. The Drama diventa così una riflessione universale sul concetto di fiducia e sul peso del "non detto". Ci costringe a chiederci se siamo davvero capaci di ascoltare e accettare il cambiamento dell'altro, o se pretendiamo una purezza utopica. La verità che il film ci sbatte in faccia è tanto complessa quanto reale: ognuno di noi custodisce zone d'ombra e segreti inconfessabili. Amare qualcuno non significa pretendere la trasparenza assoluta fin dal primo giorno, ma avere il coraggio di accogliere anche i difetti dell'altro, accettando che la conoscenza di chi ci sta accanto è un processo continuo, imperfetto e che a volte provoca dolore. Leggo alcune critiche sul fatto che il film introduca il tema delle armi per lasciarlo un po' li ma a mio parere, per quanto sia un problema di attualità in America, non è ciò su cui il regista stesso si vuole soffermare. A mio parere la volontà era più quella di dare una lettura cinica della nostra società e ci riesce anche soltanto con un personaggio secondario, Rachel, forse uno dei più odiosi che abbia mai visto negli ultimi anni e che rappresenta proprio l'ipocrisia in persona. Tu che hai quasi rischiato di ammazzare un bimbo ti ritieni superiore di una che ha pianificato una strage a 14 anni solo perché ritieni che il tuo gesto non essendo pianificato è stato meno grave del suo e non vuoi nemmeno ascoltare le motivazioni dell'altro. Ho notato poi alcune critiche focalizzate sul tema delle armi da fuoco in America lamentandone una lettura parziale. A mio parere però le armi sono solo un pretesto narrativo per allestire proprio una cinica radiografia della nostra società. La volontà credo fosse proproo far emergere una distorsione sistemica che è incarnata da uno dei personaggi più odiosi viste in un film negli ultimi anni, Rachel. Lei incarna proprio l'ipocrisia elevata a norma sociale perché la sua assenza di empatia e la sfacciata presunzione di superiorità morale creano un cortocircuito etico destabilizzante: ho davvero il diritto di condannare una mia amica per un atto pianificato a 14 anni quando io stessa ho rischiato di causare un morto pur involontariamente? Davvero sono migliore dell'altro? È quindi grazie a questi che il regista ci mostra l'inflessibilità di una società che preferisce vantarsi delle proprie virtù senza capire la reale complessità insita nel processo di crescita dell'essere umano. la potenza del regista si vede anche in quelle scene che sembrano inizialmente ridicole ma riflettendo sono tra le più dramamtiche per le persone che stanno vivendo un momento simile e che a mio parere sono piro black humor. Un film che poteva essere un banale amici amici e poi ti inculano la bici ma che riesce sia a un'interpretazione ottima degli attori che da una serie di immagini e idee di regia a veicolare un messaggio potenzialmente banale in modo molto più crudo.

Acabo de ver esta gran película y me tenía súper ansioso. Tiene unas escenas tan bien construidas que me hicieron sentir la incomodidad de los personajes y lograron que me sintiera parte del juicio moral que se estaba llevando a cabo y justo fue de las cosas que más disfruté de la película: que nunca llegué a sentirme cómodo juzgando a ninguno de los personajes porque cada vez que me quedaba claro lo que pensaba de ellos, me daba otra razón para cuestionarme. El personaje de Rachel es exquisito y muy odioso, pero hace muy bien su papel de representar ese juicio social del que todos terminamos formando parte. La película logró llevarme por un viaje donde me la pasaba preguntándome si realmente es válido el juicio social que se le está haciendo a Emma, si la actitud de Charlie es la correcta y si realmente los personajes se merecen lo que está sucediendo. Me costó llegar a este pensamiento pero después de ponerme a analizar lo que veía entendí que  justo la película hace algo más interesante que andar jugando al abogado del diablo: Primero juzgas a Emma. Después empiezas a cuestionar a Charlie. Después cuestionas a los demás. Y justo al final me di cuenta que estaba juzgando desde una posición bastante cómoda. Y ahí está una de las cosas que más disfruté, me hizo preguntarme: ¿Cuál de todas nuestras versiones somos realmente? Emma fue una adolescente capaz de planear algo terrible. Emma adulta parece ser otra persona. Charlie llega a considerarse moralmente diferente de Emma pero termina haciendo algo que contradice la imagen que tiene de sí mismo. THE DRAMA no parece afirmar que descubramos una versión “real” de nosotros mismos. Más bien parece preguntarse si somos capaces de aceptar que una persona puede contener versiones de sí misma que se contradicen. En la película esto se vuelve muy evidente durante la boda, cuando todos terminan perdiendo la cordura y esas versiones que habían construido de sí mismos empiezan a romperse. The Drama jugó con mi cabeza todo el tiempo. Cuando crees que ya sabes quién tiene la razón, te pone otra cosa enfrente y te hace volver a cuestionarlo. I firmly believe what Rachel did is way worse than what Emma did, and that is the absolute truth.   Obviously, we can't ignore the marketing, which gave the movie a massive boost because it got everyone so much more invested. The most magical thing about this film is the core dilemma it presents: what's worse, something you merely thought about doing or something you actually did? Can people genuinely change after a long period of time? Does love really conquer all? How well do you actually know the person sitting right next to you? But above all else: to what extent do you even have the right to judge?   Asking these questions, alongside the movie's absurdist tone and the various events triggered by Emma's big confession, makes the film a thousand percent intriguing. On top of that, you have this insane level of acting from the entire cast: it feels like real life drama unfold. Those arguments, Charlie's sheer fear, and Emma being so misunderstood make for a incredible watch. Emma is easily my favorite character in the film and I love her. We've already established that I adore morally questionable movies, and this one delivered on every single level. Best of all, though, is the film's ultimate message: you can always get a fresh start.
